sources.title: Sam Nixon, Excavating Essouk-Tadmakka: new archaeological investigations of early Islamic trans-Saharan trade (2009)
sources.note: Original excavation report abstract reproduced by African Union Library, directly indexed and read; DOI 10.1080/00671990903047595. 6.5 m sequence mid-first millennium to circa 1400, eighth/ninth-century extensive trade. Public copy distinguishes town evidence from nomadic camp evidence.

sources.title: Nixon, Murray and Fuller, Plant use at an early Islamic merchant town in the West African Sahel: the archaeobotany of Essouk-Tadmakka (2011)
sources.note: Primary study abstract directly read. Whole assemblage spans approximately 750 to 1400; no attribution of every taxon to eighth century. Pearl millet, dates, balanites, cotton, linseed, wheat and wild plant gathering; discussion of cultivation versus grain imports. Full article not claimed directly accessible.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, Trans-Saharan Gold Trade and Byzantine Coinage (2017)
sources.note: Full research article directly read. Section Archaeological evidence from Tadmekka discusses three low-fired clay mould fragments, horizon 6 and mid-eighth to mid-tenth-century radiocarbon interval. Author argues blanks rather than stamped coins and disputes automatic mint designation. Broad range retained, no claim they were used by 750 or by every caravan.

sources.title: Thilo Rehren and Sam Nixon, Refining gold with glass: an early Islamic technology at Tadmekka (2014)
sources.note: Full author-uploaded original paper directly read. Same work DOI 10.1016/j.jas.2014.04.013 and UCL 1431639. Section 2 dates specific crucible deposits EKA 86/87, horizon 9, to circa 900 to 1000, later than imported window. Sand-floor sequence and room of unknown function explicitly stated. Section 4 reconstructs glass-assisted mineral separation; no invention claim or proof of a workshop preserved in place.

sources.title: David Mattingly and colleagues, The origins and development of Zuwīla, Libyan Sahara (2015)
sources.note: Full original paper directly read. Same work DOI 10.1080/0067270X.2014.980126. Seventh to ninth centuries section includes 761 attack on Ibadi town; radiocarbon section dates mosque sample 670 to 857 at 95.4 percent and discusses early ninth-century architectural parallels and possible phase differences. No assertion exact construction year or uniform Islamisation.

sources.title: Münzkabinett Berlin, silver dirham of Tudgha, 173 AH (789/790), object 18278117
sources.note: Complete primary museum catalogue indexed and checked, direct HTML mostly empty/cache miss. Obverse and reverse exact scholarly Latin transliteration and German translations, mint Tudgha, AH 173, 789/790, silver 2.04 g, 27 mm, cut marks, bent and clipped. Public writing sample uses attested transliteration, not reconstructed original glyphs. Museum classifies issue in Harun al-Rashid period; no assertion caliphal sovereignty over all nomads. Tudgha is outside imported polygon; explicit nearby northern comparison.

sources.title: OECD, An Atlas of the Sahara-Sahel (2014), chapter 6, Nomadism and mobility
sources.note: Institutional field-informed synthesis, full indexed chapter passage checked, printed p. 147, Shared pastoral resources and Anchors and mobility. Direct PDF fetch failed. Explicitly contemporary comparison: individual livestock, collective wells/pastures, various fixed and mobile dwellings; not evidence of unchanged medieval customs.

proposedOverrides.name: Saharan nomadic communities
proposedOverrides.summary: Saharan mobile communities and their trading neighbors during the eighth century, with carefully dated later comparisons.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Broad imported lifeway label, distinct from prehistoric saharan-pastoral-nomads. Point checks place Essouk and Zuwīla inside; Tudgha outside and publicly labeled northern comparison. Town archaeology is explicitly neighboring context, not reclassified as nomadic camps. Plant sequence 750 to 1400 and gold crucible/floor examples circa 900 to 1000 include later evidence; OECD family/water examples explicitly 2014. Original writing is dated museum-attested Arabic transliteration, no invented glyphs or common language. No alias associations.
